(BA) has agreed to hand over its flying-taxi venture Wisk Aero to rival Archer Aviation Inc.

The divestiture marks the latest strategic move by Boeing CEO Kelly Ortberg, who took the helm in August 2024 and has spent two years working to stabilize the company's commercial airplane, defense and space operations. Ortberg has repeatedly emphasized the need to create a leaner organization. "We need to reset priorities and create a leaner, more focused organization," Ortberg said in October 2024. Last year, Boeing sold parts of its digital aviation services business — including flight-planning provider Jeppesen — to private-equity firm Thoma Bravo for $10.55 billion. The acquisition of Wisk gives Archer access to more than a decade of autonomous-flight technology.

Wisk launched in 2019 as a joint venture between Boeing and Google co-founder Larry Page's Kitty Hawk Corp., but its underlying technology had been under development for more than a decade. The company has flown six generations of eVTOLs, or electric vertical takeoff and landing aircraft.

The broader eVTOL industry has attracted billions of dollars in investment, though companies still face significant regulatory hurdles and the challenge of building out the ground infrastructure needed to support urban air-taxi networks. For Boeing, the transaction offloads subsidiaries that sit outside its primary commercial and defense operations while preserving a financial stake in a technology that could eventually transform short-distance urban travel. For Archer, absorbing Wisk's autonomous capabilities and SkyGrid's traffic management software could accelerate its path to commercial service.
